```{r}
#| include: false
# library(): loads a package so its functions can be used in this session.
# normalizePath(): resolves a path into a canonical absolute path.
# getwd(): returns the current working-directory path.
# file.exists(): checks whether each specified file path exists.
# file.path(): joins path components with the platform-appropriate separator.
# dirname(): returns the directory portion of a file path.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
library(knitr)
project <- normalizePath(getwd())
while (!file.exists(file.path(project, "20261.Rproj")) && dirname(project) != project) project <- dirname(project)
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(project, "20261.Rproj")))
```
## 1. Uniform calculation

```{r}
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# punif(): returns uniform cumulative probability between min and max; subtract CDF values for an interval.
# dunif(): returns uniform density height on min to max, not a probability at one exact point.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# names(): reads or assigns names to vector elements or table columns.
# unname(): removes names or dimension names without changing the underlying values.
a <- c(Interval_128_136=punif(136,120,140)-punif(128,120,140),Above_135=punif(135,120,140,lower.tail=FALSE),Exact_130=0,
       Density_130=dunif(130,120,140),Rounded_130=punif(130.5,120,140)-punif(129.5,120,140))
kable(data.frame(Quantity=names(a),Value=unname(a)),digits=6)
```

Probabilities: 0.40, 0.25, and 0. Density: 0.05 per minute. The nearest-minute interval corresponding to a recorded 130 has probability 0.05. Its numerical equality with the density is a consequence of that interval's width being one minute, not an equality of concepts or units.

## 2–3. Normal probabilities and cutoff

```{r}
# qnorm(): returns a normal lower-tail quantile; sd is standard deviation, not variance.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# pnorm(): returns a normal lower-tail probability; lower.tail=FALSE requests the upper tail.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# names(): reads or assigns names to vector elements or table columns.
# unname(): removes names or dimension names without changing the underlying values.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# abs(): returns absolute values; a small tolerance in an equality check permits floating-point rounding.
mu <- 36500; sigma <- 5000
z <- (40000-mu)/sigma
cutoff <- qnorm(.1,mu,sigma)
a <- c(z_score=z,Upper_tail=pnorm(40000,mu,sigma,lower.tail=FALSE),
       Standardized_tail=pnorm(z,lower.tail=FALSE),
       Interval_30000_40000=pnorm(40000,mu,sigma)-pnorm(30000,mu,sigma),
       Percentile10_miles=cutoff,Check_probability=pnorm(cutoff,mu,sigma),
       Below_30000=pnorm(30000,mu,sigma))
kable(data.frame(Quantity=names(a),Value=unname(a)),digits=6)
stopifnot(abs(pnorm(cutoff,mu,sigma)-.1)<1e-12)
```

Results: z = 0.70; upper tail 0.241964; interval 30,000–40,000 about 0.661236; cutoff about 30,092.242 miles; lower tail at 30,000 about 0.096800. `dnorm()` is a density per mile, not the upper-tail probability. The cutoff is a lifetime in miles, while a CDF value is unit-free. R's `sd` argument uses 5,000, not its square.

## 4. Plot standard

Accept an original R normal-density plot with miles on the horizontal axis, density per mile on the vertical axis, and the region above 40,000 shaded. Compare with the lesson plot. A finite display window must not be described as the model's support. Check the label says approximately 24.20%, not a density height.

## 5. Limits and the next module

A z-score rescales a variable but does not change its shape to normal. Raw road-test observations, unavailable here, would be needed to assess the fit and investigate unusual lifetimes. A sample mean is a statistic with its own sampling distribution, generally different from that of one tire; its distribution depends on the sample design and dependence among observations. Module 4 will develop this distinction. The normal model's negative tail is a mathematical limitation, even when negligible for the given parameters.
